questions.prompt: How does a Spacer behave when placed inside an HStack?

questions.prompt: Explain the three steps of the SwiftUI layout negotiation process. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains Step 1: the parent view proposes an available size to the child view.
Explains Step 2: the child view determines its own final size and reports it back.
Explains Step 3: the parent positions the child inside its coordinate space.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI layout follows a three-step negotiation process. First, the parent view proposes a size to its child view. Second, the child view determines its own size based on its contents and constraints, and reports that size back. Finally, the parent view positions the child in its coordinate space. The parent cannot force a size on the child; the child always decides its final dimensions.

questions.prompt: Compare how Spacer behaves inside an HStack versus inside a VStack. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a Spacer expands along the primary axis of its containing stack.
States that in an HStack, the Spacer expands horizontally to push siblings left and right.
States that in a VStack, the Spacer expands vertically to push siblings top and bottom.

questions.modelAnswer: A Spacer is a flexible view that expands to consume all empty space along the primary axis of its containing stack. Inside an HStack, the primary axis is horizontal, so the Spacer expands sideways to push neighboring views apart to the left and right. Inside a VStack, the primary axis is vertical, so the Spacer expands vertically to push views to the top and bottom.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens when content exceeds the size of a .frame() modifier, and describe how to clip it. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that .frame() defines proposed dimensions and alignment but does not clip content by default.
States that overflowing text or images will bleed visually outside the frame bounds.
Identifies the .clipped() modifier as the solution to cut off overflowing content.

questions.modelAnswer: Applying .frame(width:height:) defines a layout container with specific proposed dimensions, but it does not clip content by default. If child text or images exceed those dimensions, they bleed visually outside the frame bounds. Other views will still position themselves based on the frame boundaries, leading to overlapping visual bugs. To prevent content from spilling outside, you must chain the .clipped() modifier after the frame.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI distribute space among child views in an HStack when horizontal space is limited? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI offers space to the least flexible views first.
States that remaining space is divided among remaining flexible views.
Mentions that .layoutPriority(_:) can override default space allocation order.

questions.modelAnswer: When space is limited in an HStack, SwiftUI does not divide space equally. Instead, it inspects view flexibility and offers space to the least flexible views first. Once rigid views claim their required sizes, SwiftUI divides remaining space among flexible views like Spacers or text. Developers can influence this behavior by setting .layoutPriority(_:), ensuring high-priority views receive their requested space first.

questions.prompt: Explain how ZStack layers views and describe how its drawing order affects user interactions. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that ZStack renders views in sequential order from back to front along the Z-axis.
States that views declared earlier sit behind views declared later.
Explains that foreground views can block touches to background views unless configured properly.

questions.modelAnswer: ZStack layers child views depth-wise along the Z-axis from back to front. Views declared earlier in code render behind views declared later. This drawing order directly affects hit testing and user touch events. If a solid view or overlay is declared last, it sits on top and can block user taps to underlying buttons. Always place background layers first and interactive controls on top.
